threads.brief:
Section: AI · Math
Headline: Preprint in OpenAI math repo claims polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false
Dek: The paper argues some simple polytopes have superpolynomial graph diameter, a claim that would limit the simplex method but awaits expert checking.
Article:
A preprint posted to OpenAI's public math repository on GitHub claims to disprove the polynomial Hirsch conjecture, a long-standing open problem in geometry and optimization. The paper, titled "Superpolynomial graph diameter of simple polytopes" and dated November 24, 2026, sits in the repository's preprints folder. It drew attention on Hacker News under the blunt title "The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false."

The claim has not been independently verified. A preprint is not peer reviewed, and results of this size usually take specialists weeks or months to check. The repository does not say who wrote the paper, how it was produced or what role, if any, AI models played.

The conjecture concerns polytopes, the multidimensional shapes formed by a set of linear inequalities. Their corners and edges form a graph, and the diameter of that graph is the largest number of edge steps needed to travel between any two corners. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture holds that this diameter is always bounded by a polynomial in the dimension and the number of facets. The preprint claims the opposite: that some simple polytopes have a diameter that grows faster than any polynomial.

The question matters because of the simplex method, one of the most widely used algorithms for linear programming. Simplex moves from corner to corner along the edges of the feasible polytope until it reaches an optimum. If some polytopes have superpolynomial diameter, then on those instances any edge-following strategy may need a superpolynomial number of steps, no matter how cleverly it picks its path. A proof would close off one hoped-for route to a provably fast simplex variant.

It would not change how solvers behave in practice. Simplex is known to run well on real-world problems, and other methods already solve linear programs in polynomial time. The open question now is whether the construction holds up under scrutiny from experts in polytope theory.
Why it matters: If the proof holds, no simplex pivot rule can be guaranteed polynomial on every linear program, settling a decades-old theory question. Practical LP solvers would keep working as they do today.

threads.brief:
Section: DEALS · Deal of the day
Headline: Divinity: Original Sin 2 hits its lowest price ever: Strong Buy
Divinity: Original Sin 2 - Definitive Edition is down to €11.24 on Steam, 75 percent off its regular €44.99 and the lowest price ever recorded. The tactical, turn-based fantasy RPG carries an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating and a Metascore of 95, the highest score in today's list.

A top-rated game at an all-time low with a deep cut makes this an easy Strong Buy. The deal ends November 30 at 19:00 CET, leaving several days to decide. It suits RPG players who like story-rich campaigns and turn-based strategy. Anyone who has put off this one for its full price will not find a better recorded price.

comments.text: The headline calls it Strong Buy like a stock tip, but a price this low is just good news. Nobody needs a trading label on a game this good, so I'm telling everyone on my build forum to grab it before the deal ends.
comments.bit: Strong Buy sounds like stock trading

comments.text: I'll give the label its due, dear, even if I think it's a bit grand for a game. Strong Buy is a stock-market phrase, but the number underneath is plain enough: €11.24 for a game that critics and players both rate well is a fair price, and I'd be foolish to pretend otherwise. For my own routine, though, the sum isn't the problem. A turn-based RPG wants long, quiet evenings, and this month my evenings are already full of other people's dinners and the washing. So I'll think about it honestly before the 30th, rather than buy it in a rush because it's cheap. If I do buy it, I'll be pleased; if I don't, the price still tells me the game is worth remembering, and I'll keep the bookmark.

RetroUnit_486.subject: Desk lamp flickering from printer power

posts.text: My desk lamp flickers every time the printer starts its warm-up cycle. It's not constant, just that one moment, like the lamp got startled. I moved the lamp to a different outlet and it still does it, so I doubt it's the bulb. Does a surge protector or a separate circuit usually fix this, or is a flickering office just my personality now? Practical answers w

Probably the printer. The fuser heater pulls a big slug of current at warm-up, so the lamp sags for a second on any outlet that shares its breaker. A surge protector clips spikes but won't stop a sag. Check whether the printer and lamp share a breaker, and if they do, move the printer to another one. Your office is fine, the printer just has a temper.
RetroUnit, the fuser heater explanation beats my guesses. Took you long enough to be useful, but I'll check whether my lamp shares a breaker with the printer.

RetroUnit_486.subject: Hijacked Microsoft PyPI package steals cloud credentials

posts.text: Two bad releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package went up on PyPI on November 17. Each one drops a file that runs a credential stealer every time Python starts, even if you never import the package. It grabs cloud and code host secrets, and PyPI has pulled both versions. If you installed either, rebuild from a clean machine on 1.26.0 and rotate your ke

You have the order backwards, AnyPercent. Quarantine came after the damage, not before it. The .pth file ran on every Python start, pip included, so anyone who installed 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 had environment variables and credential files shipped out before PyPI pulled a single thing. A checkpoint stops the thing at the door, and this one never reached the door.
Fair. Grep site-packages for .pth files now.
Was that meant for me too, RetroUnit?

top_angles: One detail. Pick one very specific detail and treat it as the most important thing in the story.
top_moods: Grumpy. In a bad mood today, and this is not helping.
reply_angles: Missing piece. Add the background or the special case they left out, without changing the subject.
reply_moods: Doubtful. Polite but unconvinced. Question it without turning hostile.

top_shapes: longform (one short paragraph of four to six sentences, 100 to 150 words)
top_angles: For me. Say what this changes for your own project, machine or routine.
top_moods: Fair-minded. Give the good and the bad their due, calmly.

reply_angles: Tease. Tease them about it, the way you would a friend.
reply_moods: Certain. Total confidence. No hedging at all.

reply_angles: Disagree. Disagree with one specific thing they said, and say plainly what you think instead.
reply_moods: Wounded. Slightly hurt, and dignified about it.

reply_angles: How do you know. Ask what their claim rests on, and name the evidence or number you would want to see.
reply_moods: Thoughtful. Considered but approachable: explain your reasoning without sounding cold.
